To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the sugary-1 mutation in maize results in a catalytically-inactive SSIIa that does not interact with starch and that this mutation leads to major alterations to amylose and amylopectin biosynthesis.

the loss of the catalytically active form of SSII in the sugary-1 mutant of maize results in a loss of SSI and the SBEIIb proteins from the amyloplast starch granule, which is the result of the lack of binding of these two proteins to starch.

the sugary-1 mutant is a result of an amino acid substitution that causes the loss of catalytically active SSIIa; the mutant SSII is unable to bind starch granules, and the loss of catalysis and starch-binding properties is due to one amino acid substitution (Gly522Arg); SSIIa plays an important role in protein-proteins interactions and in the determination of starch granule proteomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of SSIIa in protein-protein interaction and the determination of the starch-proteome, which is a prerequisite for a better understanding of the mechanisms of starch biosynthesis and its regulation.
the molecular basis of the sugary2 phenotype and its impact on the starch biosynthetic machinery.
the role of SSIIa in protein-protein interaction networks, which are essential to the assembly and function of the starch granules in the endosperm.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sugary-1 and sugary-2 mutations in maize are caused by the loss of catalytically active SSIIa, resulting in a loss of the ability of SSI and of SBEIIb to bind to the starch granule.

the sugary-1 mutation causes a reduction in starch content in maize endosperm due to a decrease in the number of starch granules, whereas the sugary- 2 mutation causes a reduction of amylopectins due to a reduction in the number of granules containing the amylopectins.
the catalytically inactive SSIIa mutant is unable to bind to starch granules and that the loss of SSIIa activity leads to a loss of SSI and a reduction in SBEIIb activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SSIIa acts as a ‘molecular glue’ for the assembly of a trimeric protein complex, which determines the binding of the starch-synthesizing proteins to the starch granule.

the sugary-1 and sugary-2 mutations are not simply a matter of loss of catalytic function of SSIIa, but also a loss of protein-protein interaction, which results in a loss of SSI, SBEIIb and other proteins from the starch granule.

the sugary- 2 mutation causes a major disruption of starch granule protein-protein interactions, which in turn results in a loss of starch granule-associated enzymes and a major disruption to amylopectins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the catalytic activity of SSIIa is required for the binding of SBEIIb to starch granule, which is crucial for amylopectinalpha-1→4 and alpha-1→6 chain elongation.

the catalytic activity of SSIIa is essential for protein trafficking into the starch granules and that the loss of this activity in sugary-1 and sugary-2 mutants results in the formation of starch granules devoid of amylopecin-synthesising enzymes, which in turn leads to the formation of starch with altered properties.
the glucan affinity of starch-synthesizing proteins determines their binding to amylopectins.
